To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exercise stress tests can be used as a diagnostic tool in pulmonary hypertension and that they should be used in all patients with suspected disease.

(1) exercise stress testing is the only method for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension in patients with heart failure and/or valvular disease; (2) the PVR equation can be used to separate exercise-induced pulmonary hypertension due to resistance and/or flow from that due to left atrial pressure; (3) exercise stress tests are more sensitive than echocardiographic Doppler measurements for diagnosing pulmonary vascular remodelling and/or left ventricular diastsolic dysfunction.

(1) the PVR equation is the basis of the exercise stress test for the diagnosis of PH; (2) the PVR can increase as a consequence of resistance, flow, or left atrial pressure; (3) the exercise-induced PAP increase is a function of cardiac output and left atrial pressure in the normal heart and is amplified in the presence of increased PVR and left atrial pressures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the diagnosis of pulmonary vascular disease in a clinical setting, where exercise testing is used for the diagnosis and follow-up of pulmonary hypertension.
the diagnosis of PH in the presence of a normal resting PAP and a normal PAP at exercise.
the study of the relationship between the pulmonary circulation and the right heart.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a high PAP at rest is the result of a combination of high PVR, a high left atrial pressure or a high cardiac output.

the PAP response to exercise is the result of the interplay of three components: PVR, left atrial pressure and flow.3 The exercise test has been used for the assessment of pulmonary hypertension for decades.
exercise stress tests are not specific to pulmonary hypertension but may be used as an indicator of increased PAP in patients with suspected or known lung disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

exercise stress tests are useful in the assessment of pulmonary hypertension in patients with left ventricular dysfunction, and that they are not useful in patients with lung disease.3 The authors of the article in this issue of Thorax4 have used the same equation to show that exercise testing is not useful in the diagnosis of pulmonary vascular disease in patients with lung diseases.

exercise stress test is the best non-invasive tool for the diagnosis of PH and the best predictor of mortality.3–6 The most recent guidelines of the European Society of Cardiology recommend exercise stress tests as the first-line non-invasive tool to screen for the presence of pulmonary hypertension.7 In the paper of Naeije and colleagues, the authors show that exercise-induced PAP is a strong predictor of mortality.
a normal PAP–cardiovascular response to exercise is not an exclusion criterion for pulmonary hypertension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
exercise-induced PAP elevation is not necessarily a manifestation of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and may be caused by a variety of conditions.

exercise stress tests can be useful for detecting pulmonary hypertension in a variety of conditions, including left heart disease.3–5 The exercise stress test is a simple and inexpensive method for evaluating the PAP response to exercise.

a diagnosis of exercise pulmonary hypertension requires the demonstration of an elevated PAP during exercise.3–5 In defence of exercise pulmonary hypertension Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a disease of the lung circulation that is associated with a progressive increase in pulmonary artery pressure ( PAP ) and pulmonary vascular resistance ( PVR ), leading to right heart failure and death.
